card.stem: The main entrance to a dwelling house is designed to facilitate ease of access for everyone. The door shown is a high performance insulated wooden door with vertical sheeting on both sides. The door frame is 150 mm × 70 mm in cross-section and is fixed in the external wall. The wall has a 100 mm concrete block outer leaf, a 200 mm timber-frame inner leaf and a 60 mm insulated service cavity. The ground floor is an insulated solid concrete floor with a 20 mm quarry tile finish.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through the centre of the door. Show the typical construction details from 500 mm below finished floor, through the floor, the threshold, the external wall, the door and doorframe to a level 300 mm above the top of the door frame.

card.stem: The drawing shows the ground floor plan of a two-storey semi-detached house and a portion of the rear garden. The external walls of the house are 400 mm concrete block walls with a full-fill insulated cavity. The rear wall M-M is south facing. The owners need an additional space for use as a study and occasionally as a family space. The space is to have internal dimensions of 5.0 metres × 3.0 metres as shown. The following options are being considered: (i) building a single-storey extension onto the rear of the house at A. or (ii) building a detached, free-standing space in the garden at B.
card.questionText: Discuss in detail two advantages and two disadvantages of each option listed at (i) and (ii) above. — Option A

rows.contextNote: An advantage of the single-storey extension at A, discussed for this house (3). Such as: saves on construction and insulation costs; conserves space in the rear garden; more efficient energy use, as it minimises the area of external walling; more freedom in using and dividing the total living space.

A second, different advantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: easy, economical connection to existing services (space heating, plumbing, ventilation, electrical distribution); a compact plan that supports regular social interaction across the generations of the family.

A disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: disturbs the well-proportioned original layout; creates a large undifferentiated space that needs careful design; can reduce the natural lighting and ventilation of the kitchen/dining room; more energy for lighting and heating a large space.

A second, different disadvantage of the extension at A (3). Such as: fewer discrete rooms for a quieter environment; may spoil the view from the existing kitchen and dining area; continuity of insulation and weatherproofing at the roof and wall abutment; spanning the larger opening in the existing external wall may need strengthening and RSJs; misses the chance to connect the garden with the living spaces.

rows.verbatim: Two areas for upgrading - roof, windows, floor

card.questionText:
Using the following data, calculate the U-value of the external wall of a new dwelling house. The wall is of concrete block construction, with a 250 mm cavity. The cavity is a full-fill insulated cavity, with polystyrene bead insulation as shown.
Specification of external wall: external render thickness 16 mm; concrete block outer leaf thickness 100 mm; cavity width 250 mm; concrete block inner leaf thickness 100 mm; internal plaster thickness 12 mm.
Thermal data of external wall: resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m² °C/W; conductivity of external render (k) 0.720 W/m °C; conductivity of concrete blocks (k) 1.440 W/m °C; conductivity of polystyrene bead (k) 0.031 W/m °C; conductivity of internal plaster (k) 0.220 W/m °C; resistance of internal surface (R) 0.122 m² °C/W.

rows.contextNote: Use a clear resistance table or equivalent method. Convert layer thicknesses from mm to m; R = thickness/conductivity, add both surface resistances and all five material layers, then U = 1/Rtotal. The rubric heading “Insulated concrete ground floor” is a source error: the paper and the worked solution describe the specified external wall.

Seven resistances, 3 each: the five material layers by R = thickness/conductivity, with thicknesses converted from mm to m, and the two given surface resistances. External surface Rse = 0.048 (given; do not divide it by a thickness); external render 0.016/0.720 = 0.02222222; outer concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444; polystyrene bead 0.250/0.031 = 8.06451613 (the cavity is fully filled, so no separate air-cavity resistance); inner concrete-block leaf 0.100/1.440 = 0.06944444 (both leaves count); internal plaster 0.012/0.220 = 0.05454545; internal surface Rsi = 0.122 (given). All in m²·°C/W.

U = 1/Rtotal = 1/8.45017269 = 0.11834078 W/(m²·°C), approximately 0.1183 W/(m²·°C). The rubric awards 1 mark for the formula alone within this 3-mark criterion, not an additional mark. The remaining criteria stay at their own published 3-mark allocations.

card.stem: It is proposed to design the external envelope of a dwelling house to be thermal bridge free. The drawing shows an outline section through a two-storey house having a 450 mm external concrete block wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity. The roof is a traditional cut roof, the first floor has tongue-and-groove flooring on timber joists and the ground floor is an insulated solid concrete floor.
card.questionText: Select any three locations from those circled on the drawing and, using notes and freehand sketches, show best practice design detailing that will prevent the formation of a thermal bridge at each location selected.

rows.contextNote: Any three of the four circled locations, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16, showing the insulation kept continuous so that no thermal bridge forms. Junction of roof and wall at eaves: 60 mm rigid insulation board; 400 mm fibreglass insulation; a 60 mm cavity closer; an autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) block; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation. Junction of upper floors and external walls: joists hung on the inside leaf, on metal hangers or resin-anchored bolts, with no penetration of the leaf and cavity; the wall plastered for airtightness. Window cill: insulation at the back of the cill so it does not bridge the cavity; a high-density proprietary cavity closer; 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation; airtightness tape to the triple-glazed window frame. card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss in detail the importance of any two of the following in the design of a Passive House: airtight building envelope; space heating demand; indoor air quality.

rows.verbatim: Design of a Passive House - any 2
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 8 and sketches 8 = 16. Airtight building envelope: build tight and ventilate right; an unbroken air barrier on the warm side of the insulation, taped at every junction (wall/floor, wall/window, wall/door, ceiling/wall, chimney/ceiling), prevents unregulated air leakage and heat loss and lets the fresh-air intake be controlled; a service cavity keeps services from puncturing it; grommets seal pipes and cables; a blower door test checks it. Space heating demand: the energy needed to keep 20 °C indoors all year, not including hot water; a Passive House limits it to 15 kWh/m² per year or less, with a heating load of no more than 10 W/m²; the 2015 scheme also cites a primary energy demand of no more than 120 kWh/m² per year. Indoor air quality: greater airtightness needs a designed ventilation system that supplies clean, warm, filtered fresh air; mechanical ventilation with heat recovery extracts moist air from the kitchen, utility and bathrooms and passes it through a heat exchanger without mixing it with the incoming air; filters changed every three to six months; relative humidity of 30% to 60%; 0.3 to 0.6 air changes per hour.

card.stem: Light is what architecture is all about. It is as fundamental for the soul as air, fire, earth and water. Light has been one of the key elements of architecture since the Modern movement began (and glass technology improved) at the turn of the 20th century. Yet, light has traditionally been lacking in Irish homes. Many old cottages only have windows on the south side and none on the north. Now glass has improved and windows can be made with incredibly low U-values (meaning it doesn’t let the cold through), so you can now have large glazed areas without heat loss. We need light and instinctively search for it. People move to the part of the room where there is natural light and children instinctively play in pools of light.
